common_name: Chef's Choice Black Tomato (AAS-Winning Dark Beefsteak)

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Chef's Choice Black is a vigorous indeterminate beefsteak tomato in the Chef's Choice series, bred for dark, mahogany-colored fruit with rich, smoky-sweet flavor, and needs sturdy staking or caging for the large fruit.

directions: Start seeds indoors and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, staking or caging the tall indeterminate vine well before it needs the support. Chef's Choice Black is an AAS-winning beefsteak tomato bringing the dense, complex, almost smoky-sweet flavor associated with heirloom black tomatoes into a modern hybrid, with large, dusky mahogany-red-brown fruit and a meaty, low-seed interior well suited to slicing. It joins the wider Chef's Choice color series — the fruit color changes but the reliable size, disease resistance, and productivity of the line carry through. Prune suckers lightly on the lower third of the plant to improve airflow in humid climates, and mulch to keep soil moisture even, since large-fruited beefsteaks are more prone to blossom-end rot and cracking under fluctuating moisture.
sources: All-America Selections — Chef's Choice Black Tomato winner announcement

common_name: Chef's Choice Bicolor Tomato (AAS-Winning Gold-and-Pink Beefsteak)

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Chef's Choice Bicolor is a vigorous indeterminate beefsteak tomato in the Chef's Choice series, bred for streaked golden-yellow-and-pink fruit with sweet, low-acid heirloom flavor, and needs sturdy staking or caging for the large fruit.

directions: Start seeds indoors and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, staking or caging the tall indeterminate vine well before it needs the support. Chef's Choice Bicolor is an AAS-winning beefsteak tomato producing large fruit with a striking golden-yellow background streaked and blushed with rose-pink, giving each slice a marbled, sunset-like appearance on the plate as well as sweet, low-acid, heirloom-style flavor with far less of the tanginess of standard red tomatoes. It shares the reliable size, productivity, and disease resistance of the wider Chef's Choice series. Prune suckers lightly on the lower third of the plant to improve airflow in humid climates, and mulch to keep soil moisture even, since large-fruited beefsteaks are more prone to blossom-end rot and cracking under fluctuating moisture.
sources: All-America Selections — Chef's Choice Bicolor Tomato winner announcement

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; set out into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably above 55F. Icicle is a spineless white eggplant bred for long, slender fruit with fewer seeds than most white eggplant varieties.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; pick fruit young and glossy for the mildest flavor and fewest seeds. Icicle is an AAS-winning eggplant producing long, slender, pure-white fruit on spineless plants, a genuine convenience for hand-harvesting compared to the sharp spines that guard the calyx of many eggplant varieties. It carries noticeably fewer seeds than typical white eggplant, giving a creamier, less bitter texture, and its tender skin needs no peeling. The productive, well-branched plants set fruit reliably over a long summer season. Harvest regularly while fruit is still glossy and firm, since letting fruit overripen on the plant both reduces quality and slows further production; the plant responds to frequent picking with a steady stream of new fruit through the season.
sources: All-America Selections — Icicle Eggplant winner announcement

common_name: Profusion Red Zinnia (AAS-Winning Disease-Resistant Heat-Proof Single Zinnia)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost when soil is consistently warm (70F+) in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Profusion Red was bred for the same powdery-mildew resistance and heat tolerance as the rest of the Profusion series, which was bred to hold up in Gulf South summer humidity where standard large-flower zinnias typically fail.

directions: Direct sow after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Profusion Red is an AAS-winning member of the Profusion zinnia series (Zinnia marylandica, a hybrid between Z. elegans and Z. angustifolia), bred for the same powdery mildew resistance and heat tolerance as its Profusion Orange and Profusion White stablemates, producing abundant clean, single, deep-red flowers on a compact, bushy, mounding plant that keeps healthy foliage through a full Gulf South summer that would defoliate a standard large-flowered zinnia. It is self-cleaning, dropping spent flowers without deadheading, and blooms continuously from planting through frost. Its compact scale and continuous color make it a dependable choice for garden edges, mass plantings, and containers, and the flowers draw butterflies heavily throughout the season.
sources: All-America Selections — Profusion Red Zinnia winner announcement

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Double Delight is an AARS 1977 winner bred by Swim & Ellis and benefits from preventative fungicide application and consistent feeding in humid climates.

directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Double Delight is a landmark hybrid tea rose, an All-America Rose Selections winner in 1977, celebrated for its striking bicolor blooms — creamy white petals that develop a vivid strawberry-red edge that deepens with sun exposure and age, so a single bush shows blooms in varying stages of color at once. Its heavy, intense, spicy-sweet fragrance is considered among the finest of modern roses, making it a favorite for cutting as well as garden display. Like many hybrid teas from this era, it needs a regular preventative fungicide program in humid, disease-prone climates to keep the foliage healthy through summer. Prune hard in late winter, feed with rose fertilizer monthly through the growing season, and deadhead spent blooms to encourage continued flowering.
sources: World Federation of Rose Societies — Rose Hall of Fame

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Julia Child is an AARS 2006 winner bred by Tom Carruth and noted for strong disease resistance for a floribunda, needing less spraying than many older rose varieties.

directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Julia Child is a floribunda rose named for the famous chef with the blessing of the Julia Child Foundation, an All-America Rose Selections winner in 2006 prized for its rich, buttery-gold, ruffled double flowers produced in generous clusters, along with a distinctive licorice-and-clove fragrance unlike most other roses. It is notably more disease-resistant than many older rose varieties, holding clean, glossy foliage with less spraying, which makes it a good choice for gardeners who want strong rose performance without a heavy maintenance program. The compact, well-branched, floriferous habit suits both mixed borders and mass plantings. Prune in late winter, feed with rose fertilizer through the growing season, and deadhead to encourage the next flush of the repeat bloom cycle.
sources: World Federation of Rose Societies — Rose Hall of Fame

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Chrysler Imperial is an AARS 1953 winner bred by Walter Lammerts and, like many classic hybrid teas, benefits from a preventative fungicide program in humid climates.

directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Chrysler Imperial is a classic hybrid tea rose, an All-America Rose Selections winner in 1953, celebrated for its large, velvety, deep-crimson double flowers and an intense, old-rose fragrance that earned it the James Alexander Gamble Fragrance Medal in 1965 — one of the highest honors in rose fragrance. Its rich color and heavy scent made it a mid-century garden and florist standard, and it remains a favorite where classic hybrid tea form and strong perfume matter more than the disease resistance of modern landscape roses. As with most older hybrid teas, expect to manage black spot and powdery mildew with a regular preventative spray program in humid, rainy climates. Prune hard in late winter, feed monthly through the growing season, and deadhead spent blooms to keep the repeat-flowering cycle going.
sources: World Federation of Rose Societies — Rose Hall of Fame

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Tropicana is an AARS 1963 winner bred by Mathias Tantau and one of the best-selling roses of the 20th century, though like many older hybrid teas it benefits from a preventative fungicide program in humid climates.

directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Tropicana, also sold as Super Star, is a landmark hybrid tea rose bred in Germany and released to enormous acclaim in the early 1960s, celebrated for its almost fluorescent coral-orange color — a shade so vivid it was said to have been a genuine breeding breakthrough at the time — carried on large, high-centered blooms with a strong, fruity fragrance. It became one of the best-selling roses of the 20th century and remains a benchmark for vivid orange rose color. As with most classic hybrid teas, expect to manage black spot and powdery mildew with a regular preventative spray program in humid climates. Prune hard in late winter, feed monthly through the growing season, and deadhead spent blooms to sustain the repeat-flowering cycle.
sources: World Federation of Rose Societies — Rose Hall of Fame

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Tuff Stuff is a Proven Winners mountain hydrangea that flowers on both old and new wood, giving it a much longer rebloom window and better resistance to losing a season's flowers to a late spring freeze than bigleaf hydrangeas that bloom on old wood only.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with some protection from hot afternoon sun; Tuff Stuff is a compact reblooming mountain hydrangea (Hydrangea serrata) bred by Proven Winners to flower on both old and new growth, so even if a hard late freeze damages the previous year's buds, the plant still produces a strong flush of lacecap blooms on new wood later in the season — a real advantage over bigleaf hydrangeas that bloom only on old wood and can lose an entire year's flowering to a bad spring frost. Flower color shifts with soil pH, from blue in acidic soil to more pink or purple tones in neutral to alkaline soil, the same way it does in bigleaf hydrangea. Mountain hydrangea is generally more cold-hardy and sun-tolerant than bigleaf hydrangea, and its compact size fits well into smaller foundation plantings and mixed shrub borders. Water regularly during dry spells, since hydrangeas wilt quickly in dry soil, and mulch to keep roots cool and moist through summer heat.
